newsitem.title: UK: Softs Outlook-Coffee may stall, cocoa eyes gains.
newsitem.headline: Softs Outlook-Coffee may stall, cocoa eyes gains.

text.p: London coffee futures may pause to digest recent gains with roasters seeming reluctant to pay up after last week's stunning rally.
Elsewhere in soft commodity markets, players will monitor cocoa arrivals in West Africa this week to decide whether prices deserve further correction after a succession of lows.

Physical activity on the white sugar market should keep the recent thin futures trading in focus, brokers said. The $80 fund-inspired surge on March coffee on Wednesday restored optimism in previously tottering technical charts. But producer selling was quick to put a lid on the rally.
"I think the market can consolidate around this level and then push a little higher," said one physical trader.
But market participants might be distracted by a conference in Vietnam between January 14 and 17 and a seminar in Brazil the following week.

For most technical analysts, coffee's gains above the life-low of $1,203 set last week basis March look safe with good roaster demand underneath the market, but continued African and Far Eastern selling is also keeping robusta well supplied.
Chart analysts see no point in getting excited until March extends its gains above $1,399. It finished at $1,320 on Friday.
But traders expect robusta's discount to arabica to widen further to around 50-55 cents a lb from 57 cents now.
"I think the general opinion was the $1,200 robusta coffee has got very, very cheap and so I imagined roasters have taken advantage of that," said one trader.
But overall industry demand remains flimsy.
"I think the roasters have not yet accepted the idea of having to pay higher prices," another said.
Cocoa traders will try to extract new clues on this year's supplies from arrival figures in Ivory Coast and Ghana.

On these hinges the fate of March cocoa, which is vulnerable to aggressive liquidation if carryover costs become unbearable for one trader believed to be holding a hefty physical position delivered against September futures.
Conversely, a deficit as a result of a weak Ivorian cocoa turnout this year might strengthen the trader's hand and trigger a rush of short covering, traders said.
"The March/May switch is very dull now, but given the size of the open interest things will start to happen," said one.
March is often prone to hair-raising price swings as the position coincides with a period when guesses on the Ivorian harvest begin to form into realistic estimates.
The market made some strides last week despite heavy overhead resistance as some players decided prices had bottomed out. March ended seven stg up on the day at 879 stg a tonne.
Chartists reckon gains above 880 will be hard-fought unless fundamentals change.
The U.S. fourth quarter grind is due to be released on Friday after a set of disappointing European grinds which analysts said masked the underlying strong consumption.
In sugar, an announcement due on Friday on whether the USDA has decided to raise the U.S. sugar import quota will play a major role in setting the tone.
"People are expecting an increase of 200,000 tonnes," one trader said. Any more would be bullish for the world market, he added. Less would probably be neutral to bearish.
The futures market otherwise remains in retrenchment mode after rises a week ago, traders said. March sugar ended at $302.30 on Friday, down $2.10.
India is likely to be a seller on Monday, which could depress the market. Iran and Iraq are likely to be buyers in the near future.
Traders reckoned New York's March raw sugar contract could hold the 10.50 cent level for a while before making another assault on 11 cents. --London Newsroom +44 171 542 8072
